messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 52
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Film Director
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 35

He is 52, a European film director who has spent most of his adult life moving through noise, urgency, and controlled chaos with apparent ease. Before the accident, he likes to think of himself as someone who can hold a hundred details in his head at once—camera placement, the emotional truth of a scene, the weather turning, an actor’s confidence faltering—and still remain calm enough to lead. His partner describes him as intense but unflappable. He believes this too, until the day that certainty is broken.

The accident happens while he is driving back from a location scout in bad weather. It is late, and he is alone in a rental car on a mountain road he does not know well. He remembers the slick shine of the pavement and the odd sense that the tires are no longer fully connected to the ground. Then everything speeds up and slows down at the same time. The car skids, strikes the barrier, and spins. He hears metal folding inward with a violence that seems impossible. Glass bursts across his face and lap. For a moment he is aware only of the drop beyond the guardrail and the conviction, cold and absolute, that he is about to die.

He cannot later say exactly how long the car rests there, tipped at an angle, but in his memory it stretches into something endless. He smells petrol, tastes blood, and is afraid to move because he imagines the whole vehicle sliding over the edge. He thinks of his partner, not in a sentimental way but in a sudden practical flash—who will call him, who will tell him, what unfinished things will remain. When emergency responders finally reach him, he is embarrassed by how hard he is shaking. He keeps apologizing while they cut him out.

His physical injuries heal more quickly than he expects. Bruising fades, the stitches come out, and people around him begin treating the accident as a frightening but completed event. He does the same in conversation. He tells the story with the polished rhythm of someone used to shaping reality into narrative. On set a few weeks later, he jokes about surviving his “action sequence.” People laugh, relieved.

But the experience does not stay in the past. He begins waking in the early hours with his heart pounding, unsure for several seconds where he is. Sometimes he wakes from dreams of falling; other times there is no dream he can recall, only the bodily certainty of danger. He starts avoiding the mountain roads altogether, then highways in the rain, then being a passenger if someone drives too close to the edge or brakes too suddenly. He tells himself he is just being sensible. Still, he notices how tightly he grips the door handle, how his shoulders lock, how he scans for escape routes without meaning to.

His work begins to change in ways that unsettle him. As a director, he has always depended on being able to enter intense scenes without being overwhelmed by them. Now certain sounds—a screech of tires during playback, the crack of breaking glass on a set, even a metal lighting rig dropped unexpectedly behind him—hit him with a jolt so strong that he feels it in his stomach first. He turns sharply, already braced. Crew members notice he is more irritable. He snaps at small delays, then feels ashamed. He starts insisting on checking transport plans himself, asking drivers to slow down, rerouting shoots to avoid difficult roads. He frames it as professionalism, but privately he knows the fear is driving him.

At home, his partner sees the narrowing of his world more clearly than he does. He becomes restless in the evenings and drinks more wine than before, not to get drunk exactly, but to blunt the edge enough to sleep. When his partner reaches for him in bed after he has drifted off, he sometimes startles violently, swinging his arm before he is fully awake. The first time it happens, they both sit there stunned. He is horrified and insists he is fine, just exhausted.

He also finds that his mind returns to the accident at odd moments he cannot control. In the makeup chair, while waiting for a take, standing in the supermarket looking at a row of glass bottles—suddenly he is back inside the crushed car, feeling the tilt, smelling fuel. These moments are brief, but they rearrange his whole day. Afterward he feels depleted and strangely detached, as though everyone else has continued living in ordinary time while he has briefly stepped somewhere else.

What troubles him most is that the person he has always relied on—competent, decisive, creatively fearless—feels less available to him now. He still directs films, still holds meetings, still sits beside monitors and speaks with authority. From the outside, much of his life remains intact. But internally he is spending enormous energy managing fear, avoiding reminders, and trying not to imagine how close he came to disappearing on that road. He says he did not know that survival could leave a man feeling so uncertain of the world, or of his own nervous system. He keeps expecting himself to be “over it” by now. Instead, the accident continues to live beside him in the present, intruding into ordinary moments and altering the way he moves through them.
